reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: X-linked overgrowth syndrome affecting predominantly males, with pre- and postnatal macrosomia and organomegaly
Coarse facial features include a broad face, hypertelorism, a broad nasal bridge, macrostomia, and a midline groove or furrow of the tongue and lower lip
Associated malformations include congenital heart disease, diaphragmatic hernia, polydactyly, supernumerary nipples, and genitourinary anomalies
Caused by loss-of-function variants or deletions in GPC3 (with GPC4 involvement in some) on the X chromosome
X-linked recessive inheritance, so carrier females are usually mildly affected or unaffected while males are more severely affected
Carries an increased risk of embryonal tumours, particularly Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma, warranting tumour surveillance in childhood
Overlaps clinically with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome but is distinguished by X-linked inheritance and the specific facial and skeletal features
reference.pathophysiology: Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome arises from loss of function of GPC3, an X-linked gene encoding glypican-3, a cell-surface heparan sulfate proteoglycan that modulates growth factor signalling and helps restrain cell proliferation during development, in part by regulating hedgehog and IGF-related pathways. Absent or reduced glypican-3 removes this brake on tissue growth, producing generalised overgrowth, organomegaly, and a predisposition to embryonal tumours, while disturbed developmental signalling accounts for the structural malformations and characteristic facies.
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing for GPC3 sequence variants and deletions, with GPC4 analysis and overgrowth panel where indicated
Chromosomal microarray to detect Xq26 deletions
Abdominal ultrasound as part of embryonal tumour surveillance
Serum alpha-fetoprotein monitoring for hepatoblastoma surveillance in early childhood
Echocardiography and renal tract imaging for structural anomalies
Skeletal survey and evaluation for diaphragmatic hernia and polydactyly
redFlags: New abdominal mass, haematuria, or rising alpha-fetoprotein suggesting Wilms tumour or hepatoblastoma
Respiratory distress from diaphragmatic hernia in the neonatal period
Cardiac decompensation from structural heart disease
Neonatal hypoglycaemia or arrhythmia requiring urgent management
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity of malformations and tumour occurrence; severe cases may present with neonatal complications, while milder cases have a favourable outlook with appropriate surveillance. Early detection of embryonal tumours through structured screening improves outcomes.
pitfalls: Confusing the syndrome with Beckwith-Wiedemann and thereby overlooking X-linked inheritance and carrier risk to relatives
Omitting embryonal tumour surveillance in a child with overgrowth and organomegaly
Underestimating disease in carrier females who may show subtle features
Missing a diaphragmatic hernia or cardiac lesion in the newborn assessment
